subject: Business
title: Disruption from Below
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Disruption from Below.

hook.text: Mini steel mills made cheap, low-quality rebar. Big mills ignored them. Then mini mills ate the whole industry.

buildup.text: Disruption from below starts in the least attractive market segment — the one incumbents happily abandon.

discovery.text: The disruptor's product improves over time. What starts as 'not good enough' becomes 'good enough and cheaper.'

twist.text: Incumbents rationally retreat upmarket each time. Every step up feels profitable — until there's nowhere left to go.

climax.text: Toyota entered the US with cheap, small cars. Detroit laughed. Toyota is now the world's largest automaker.

punchline.text: If you're ignoring the low end, someone is building your replacement.

quiz.question: Where does disruption from below typically start?
options: In the least attractive market segment incumbents abandon
At the premium end of the market

details.summary: Disruption from below occurs when a low-cost, simpler product enters at the bottom of a market and gradually improves until it displaces established players serving the mainstream. Incumbents typically dismiss the disruptors as inferior until it is too late to respond.
details.whyItMatters: Clayton Christensen's disruption theory explains why successful companies fail despite doing everything right by their best customers.
takeaways: Disruptors enter with inferior but cheaper products serving overlooked segments
They improve rapidly until their product satisfies mainstream customers
Incumbents rationally ignore disruptors because margins look unattractive

faq.question: Why do successful companies fail to respond to disruption?
faq.answer: Their best customers demand higher-end features with better margins. Investing in low-end products cannibalize existing revenue. Resource allocation processes favor serving profitable existing customers. By the time the disruptor reaches the mainstream, it is too late to catch up.

faq.question: What is a classic example of disruption from below?
faq.answer: Minicomputers disrupted mainframes, then PCs disrupted minicomputers. Digital cameras disrupted film. Each new entrant was initially worse on performance metrics that incumbents valued but offered simplicity, convenience, or cost that attracted new or underserved users.
